A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same local SIFT-flow seam-repair work despite the changed title and presentation. All pages, equations, figures, tables and references are readable; neither supplied PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: v1 reports original stitching-quality and runtime evaluations on three datasets, visual comparisons, and a 20-participant preference study in Section 4.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations with and without LPAM, including seam quality, global alignment and runtime results in Tables I–III, plus visual comparisons and failure examples.

M1.justification: The specified seam-evaluation score changes from D[(1−SSIM)/2] in v1 Eq. (2) to 1−SSIM in v2 Eq. (2), omitting the denoising operation used to suppress small misalignments. The core thresholding, SIFT-flow alignment, sigmoid modification and seam-merging procedure remains; naming it LPAM does not itself introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions retain 35 Parallax pairs, 24 SEAGULL pairs and the same 20-pair authors' dataset, verified against the dataset illustrations. v2 removes the separate human perceptual-ranking task and participant population described in v1 Section 4.3, without substantially expanding image-domain coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds the Euclidean Baseline and Quaternion methods to the retained Perception and Iterative comparisons, evaluating all four with and without LPAM in Tables I–III. Photomerge disappears from the visual comparisons, while Microsoft ICE, Parallax and SEAGULL remain. This substantially changes the evaluated comparator set.

E3.justification: Initial alignment changes from triangular-facet approximation in v1 Section 4 to robust elastic warping in v2 Section IV. Evaluation expands from one SSIM-derived seam error to RMSE, PSNR, SSIM and ZNCC, with additional whole-overlap alignment measurements and paired LPAM controls. Timing separates LPAM overhead and uses different hardware; the human-ranking protocol is removed.

E4.justification: v2 extends the with/without local-alignment comparison across four seam cutters and adds the global-alignment diagnostic in Table II. Figure 7 examines missed detection of broadly defective seams and inadequate smoothing within small patches, replacing v1's large-displacement failure example. The iteration-count/patch-count analysis in v1 Figure 9 disappears, while the beta sensitivity illustration is retained as v2 Figure 3.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests or uncertainty estimates. The removed preference-vote totals and newly tabulated aggregate scores are results, not changes in uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v1's per-image quality plots and preference scores—514 for the proposed method, 340 for Perception and 266 for Iterative—are removed. v2 Tables I–III introduce extensive seam-quality, global-alignment and separate LPAM-runtime results; for example, Parallax seam SSIM is 0.749 for Perception and 0.795 with LPAM. These are newly reported comparisons under revised settings, not demonstrated performance gains from v1 to v2.

T1.justification: Eq. (2) revises the mathematical definition of seam error by removing denoising and rescaling the SSIM difference. The correspondence assumption, graph-cut objective, sigmoid and seam-boundary constraints remain. v2's explicit warped-patch equation mainly formalizes the existing operation; neither version contains theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 drops v1's explicit contribution claim that the method can 'almost remove' the rough-alignment assumption. Its abstract and contributions emphasize effective, efficient improvement through a plug-in module. The central large-parallax stitching objective and claimed applicability to other seam-cutting methods were already present in v1.

C2.justification: v1 explains widespread seam failure as potentially requiring impractical alignment of the entire overlap. v2 instead identifies how the relative-error acceptance rule can declare a badly aligned seam plausible and extract no patches, and adds an alignment-versus-smooth-merging limitation for small patches. It also removes v1's discussion of average seam scores disagreeing with perceived quality, substantially revising the interpretation of failures and evaluation limits.

D1.justification: v2 newly identifies MATLAB implementation and reports dataset availability with code at an updated repository, whereas v1 promises a future code release. Reported hardware changes from a 3.4 GHz i7 with 32 GB memory to a 3.6 GHz i7 with 16 GB. Patch size, k and beta remain unchanged, while v1's explicit statement about using comparator default settings is omitted.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of quaternion-domain stitching and dense-matching seam estimation, expands discussion of the previously cited edge-guided composition network, and adds survey references. Several earlier citations, including ISGTA and older blending work, disappear. The established seam-cutting/seam-driven organization and basic positioning against fixed prealignment remain.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, contribution paragraphs and conclusion are rewritten around LPAM. The method's five subsections are consolidated into a preliminary and two stages, while the experimental narrative is reorganized around paired module evaluations and a separate efficiency subsection. These are extensive language and structural changes beyond renaming.

P2.justification: v2 introduces a pipeline overview, replaces per-image quality and timing plots with structured tables, redesigns visual comparisons into paired panels, and replaces the failure display. The retained beta illustration is rearranged into four labeled panels. Typography, author block, captions and page layout also change throughout.

improvement.justification: The paired evaluations across four seam cutters better support applicability beyond v1's Perception-based implementation, and the global-alignment diagnostic and more precise failure analysis improve explanation. However, removing the human-preference study and per-image diagnostics weakens perceptual and case-level evidence. These tradeoffs support a limited net improvement rather than a substantial overall gain.
